description: Hi! I'm Kasem, a Computer Engineering student at Mansoura University . We're tackling "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map", helping future astronauts explore Mars safely using NASA mission data.
summary:
Ariadne is a web app that helps the first astronauts on Mars plan a safe walk to science targets. It covers a 5 × 5 km area of Mount Sharp in Gale Crater, where NASA's Curiosity rover is exploring today.

Ariadne combines data from several NASA missions into one layered map: a 1 m elevation model and HiRISE color images (Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter), THEMIS thermal inertia (Mars Odyssey) to tell sand from rock, and Curiosity's route, photos and REMS weather. The astronaut clicks a start point and science targets. Ariadne finds the safest walking route with an A* search that avoids steep slopes, sand and cliffs, and picks the best order to visit the targets. It shows distance, climb, walking time, radiation dose, the weather for the sol, and a go/no-go check against the suit's time limit. A 3D terrain view and an astronaut's-eye walk, showing real Curiosity photos of the view ahead, let the crew see the route before they step outside.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
Ariadne plans a safe walk for astronauts on Mount Sharp, Gale Crater, the area NASA's Curiosity rover is exploring today. The name comes from Ariadne's thread: the safe line that leads you through the maze and back. The astronaut places a start point and up to a few science targets (for example the boxwork formations) on a 5 x 5 km map. Ariadne then:
- finds the safest walking route and the best order to visit the targets;
- shows distance, elevation gain, walking time, radiation dose and the weather for the sol;
- gives a go/no-go check (for example: does the whole walk, including work time at each target, fit inside a 4-hour suit limit?);
- lets the crew compare the "fastest" and "safest" route side by side with a priority slider;
- plays the walk back in 2D, in 3D terrain, or from the astronaut's own eyes, with a helmet display;
- shows real Curiosity photos taken near each stop, and in the astronaut view the Curiosity photo of the direction you are looking.

HOW IT WORKS
1. Data preparation (Python, rasterio): our script crops every NASA dataset to the same 5 x 5 km area and puts them on one grid. From the 1 m elevation model we compute slope; from THEMIS thermal inertia we estimate how sandy the ground is (low thermal inertia = loose sand).
2. Cost map: each 5 m cell gets a walking cost. Slope under 10 degrees is easy, 10-15 hard, 15-25 very hard, over 25 degrees blocked, and any 1 m spot steeper than 35 degrees (cliff or boulder) blocks its cell. Cost = 1 + 150 x (slope/25)^2 + 50 x sandiness.
3. Route search: our own A* search (JavaScript, in the browser) finds the cheapest path between every pair of points, then picks the best visiting order. A 3-target route plans in under half a second. The routing code has automated unit tests.
4. Mission numbers: walking speed depends on slope; radiation uses 0.64 mSv per day measured on the surface by Curiosity's RAD instrument (Hassler et al., 2014); weather comes from Curiosity's REMS station; a sol is 24.66 hours.
5. Views: a Leaflet map with layers you can switch on and off (colour photo, slope, sand and rock, Curiosity's route), a three.js 3D terrain view with 30 km of surroundings, a Mars globe you fly down from, and a first-person astronaut walk.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT
Before a real Marswalk, a crew must know: can we get there safely, how long will it take, how much radiation will we get, and what will we see? Today that answer is spread across many separate NASA datasets. Ariadne puts them in one place and turns them into a route and a clear go/no-go answer. The same method works for any landing site that has an elevation model and orbital images, so it could help plan the first human walks on Mars, and it is a simple way for students and the public to explore real Mars data.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE
- Real Curiosity photos placed in the 3D world: we use the camera pointing data in NASA's raw-image records so the astronaut sees the actual photo of the direction they are facing.
- Fastest vs. safest comparison instead of a single "best" route.
- A full mission flow: briefing, planning, go/no-go, and a walk-through, plus a guided tour for first-time users.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED
Slope and cliffs, loose sand (rovers have got stuck in it), total time against suit limits, work time at each target, radiation dose, temperature and pressure for the sol, and keeping the app light enough to run in any browser with no installation.

TOOLS
HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no framework), Leaflet, three.js, Chart.js, Python with rasterio and NumPy, GitHub Pages.

USE OF AI
Code was written with help from Claude (Anthropic), an AI coding assistant, and reviewed and tested by our team. All data and images in the app are real NASA data; none are AI-generated. This is also noted in the project's README.
